title: India Meets Fiscal Deficit Target for FY26 as Credit Ratings Improve, Sitharaman Says
excerpt: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman told the Indian diaspora in Chicago that India achieved its fiscal deficit goal of 4.4% of GDP for 2025-26 and is targeting a debt-to-GDP ratio of 50% by 2030.
body:
• India's fiscal deficit came in at 4.4% of GDP for FY26, meeting the government's planned consolidation trajectory, Finance Minister Sitharaman confirmed.
  • The government is targeting a debt-to-GDP ratio of 50% by 2030, compared with levels above 200% in several advanced economies.
  • India's GDP has grown at 7% or above since the pandemic despite disruptions from the Russia-Ukraine war, tariff disputes, and shipping corridor instability.
  • India is pursuing bilateral trade agreements with the EU, Australia, UAE, and EFTA nations as multilateral trade frameworks stall.

India has met its fiscal deficit target for 2025-26, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Sunday while addressing the Indian diaspora in Chicago, asserting that the government has stayed on course with its planned fiscal consolidation.

"We have given ourselves a fiscal discipline path on the fiscal deficit as well. We have fulfilled the trajectory. The last mile that had to be reached by 2025-26, we have reached," Sitharaman said.

India's fiscal deficit stood at 4.4% of GDP for the year ended March 31, 2026. In absolute terms, it was Rs 15.19 trillion, coming in at 97.5% of the government's revised estimate presented in February.

Debt-to-GDP Target of 50% by 2030

Sitharaman addressed concerns over government borrowing, saying the administration is targeting a debt-to-GDP ratio of 50% by 2030. She compared India's position with several advanced economies where debt levels exceed 200% of GDP.

"The fiscal prudence shall not be compromised. As a result, credit ratings are improving."

— Nirmala Sitharaman, Finance Minister of India

The finance minister said the government had maintained fiscal discipline without cutting funding for social welfare programs or reducing public capital expenditure on infrastructure — a balancing act that has drawn attention from credit rating agencies in recent years.

Growth Resilience Through Global Turbulence

Sitharaman pointed to India's post-pandemic economic performance, noting that domestic growth has remained at 7% or above despite a series of global headwinds, including the Russia-Ukraine war, escalating trade tariff disputes, and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz shipping corridor.

On the supply side, the minister highlighted the government's handling of fertiliser procurement during volatile commodity markets. International urea prices surged tenfold after the pandemic, from Rs 300 to Rs 3,000 per bag. The government absorbed the entire price increase through a subsidy of Rs 2,700 per bag, Sitharaman said.

She added that the government stepped in with budgetary support after international insurance providers declined to cover vessels traveling through volatile transit corridors, covering higher risk premiums for shipping liners to ensure imports continued without disruption.

Bilateral Trade Push as Multilateralism Slows

On the trade front, Sitharaman said India is continuing to pursue bilateral agreements with the European Union, Australia, the UAE, and EFTA nations, as multilateral frameworks have stalled.

"Trade agreements are continuing. On a bilateral basis, we are moving with trade treaties. The multilateral treaty age has gone off," Sitharaman said.

The finance minister is in Chicago as part of a nine-day official visit to Canada and the United States from August 25 to September 2. The U.S. leg began on August 28. She is scheduled to attend G20 finance track meetings in Asheville, North Carolina, following bilateral economic dialogues in Canada.

Fiscal Discipline as Market Signal

Meeting the fiscal deficit target reinforces India's position among emerging markets where fiscal credibility has become a differentiator. The combination of sustained capital spending and deficit reduction offers a measure of predictability that foreign institutional investors and sovereign wealth funds have increasingly valued, particularly as several large economies contend with rising debt burdens and slowing growth.
